newsitem.title: CANADA: Freed Cuban dissident poet comes to Canada.
newsitem.headline: Freed Cuban dissident poet comes to Canada.

text.p: A prominent Cuban dissident writer, who arrived in Canada on Sunday after his sudden release from a Cuban prison, vowed on Monday to continue speaking out against Communist rule in Cuba.

Cecilio Ismael Sambra Haber, a 49-year-old poet, said in a telephone interview from the southern Ontario city of Waterloo that he could not remain indifferent to the "bad things that are happening in Cuba."

"It is important to speak against the tyranny that the Cuban people are suffering at the moment," Sambra said through an interpreter. "While I am alive, I will continue to give testimony to this tyranny."
Sambra arrived in Waterloo on Sunday with his wife, Marta Rios, and two children, Yasmine, 11, and Yasiel, 5, to begin a two-year stay as a writer-in-exile at Wilfrid Laurier University.
Another son, Guiilermo, remained in prison in Cuba.
Sambra's release last Friday capped a five-year odyssey that began when the poet was arrested during Cuba's 1992 elections for distributing pamphlets that read, "No to Castro -- vote for freedom."
Sentenced to 10 years in the notorious Boniato prison near Santiago in eastern Cuba, Sambra said he lived a life tinged by hunger strikes, ill health and profound loneliness.
"It was the most hurtful place in the world to be," Sambra said.
PEN Canada, a writers' organization that works on behalf of writers imprisoned or harassed for expressing themselves, "adopted" Sambra's case last year.
PEN officials called Sambra's release a rare success story.
"We have various cases we're looking it. We just got lucky in this case," said Isobel Harry, PEN policy director.
Canada's Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy, who brought up Sambra's case with Fidel Castro during a state visit in January, said the release was promising.
Axworthy said Canada was succeeding in its efforts to move the Cuban regime toward a greater respect for human rights.
The human rights group Amnesty International estimated last year that there were 600 prisoners of conscience and several hundred political prisoners in Cuba.
